clue.text: Hope network's designed to be aware of best practice

indicators.note: something designed has been planned and arranged anew, so the letters are set out in a fresh order

blocks.note: twelve letters taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A charity or support network has been set up so that it follows the best practice in its field.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole of 'Hope network's' is the raw material, apostrophe-S included; 'designed' tells you to rearrange it into KNOW THE ROPES.
explanation.definitionFit: To know the ropes is an idiom for being familiar with how things are properly done, originally from sailors handling rigging.

clue.text: African nation, one with capital in Abuja?

definitions.text: African nation, one with capital in Abuja

indicators.note: a capital letter heads a word, so only the opening letter of the next word is wanted

blocks.note: a landlocked country in West Africa
the Roman numeral for one
the opening letter of the city's name

explanation.surface: A quiz question asking which African country has Abuja as its capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer, since Abuja is the capital of NIGERIA, while also building it: neighbouring NIGER, then I, then A.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigeria is a West African country whose seat of government moved from Lagos to Abuja in 1991.

clue.text: The Observer embracing Right, that is most odd

indicators.note: to embrace is to wrap one's arms around, so one part goes inside another

blocks.note: a newspaper speaks of itself in its editorials as 'we'
the Latin id est, abbreviated i.e., means 'that is'
the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A claim that The Observer, Britain's liberal Sunday paper, taking in right-wing views would be the strangest thing of all.
explanation.walkthrough: A newspaper's editorials speak as 'we'; 'that is' must be expanded to the full Latin id est rather than the usual i.e. abbreviation, with right placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Weird and odd are synonyms, so the superlative weirdest means most strange or peculiar.

clue.text: Uttered casual greeting, being drunk

indicators.note: something uttered is spoken, so only its sound matters, not its spelling

blocks.note: an informal hello, said out loud

explanation.surface: Someone tipsy calling out a cheery hello to everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: Say the informal greeting HI and you hear HIGH, which is the word wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: High is informal for intoxicated, whether by alcohol or drugs, so it stands in for tipsy or inebriated.

clue.text: Newspaper, Independent, covers no-good rubbish boxing movie

blocks.note: rag is slang for a low-quality newspaper
I is the standard abbreviation for independent
NG is the abbreviation for no good
bull is slang for nonsense

explanation.surface: The Independent newspaper reviews a poor boxing film and pans it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newspaper, Independent' looks like one paper's name, but it is two pieces, RAG and I; 'covers' simply joins them to the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Raging Bull is Martin Scorsese's 1980 film about the boxer Jake LaMotta, played by Robert De Niro.

clue.text: Primarily: poet (... listed alongside Ted Hughes?)

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the leading letter of each following word is taken

blocks.note: the initial letters of the five words

explanation.surface: An anthology entry: a poet whose name appears beside Ted Hughes's.
explanation.walkthrough: The heads of 'poet listed alongside Ted Hughes' spell PLATH, and the whole phrase also describes her, since Sylvia Plath was Hughes's wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Sylvia Plath, American poet, married the English Poet Laureate Ted Hughes, and their names are constantly paired in literary history.

clue.text: Perhaps pens epistle, angry initially in Welsh city

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so just the opening letters of the preceding words are used

blocks.note: a pen is a female swan, so pens are an example of these birds
the leading letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone in a Welsh city furiously writing a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pens' looks like a verb about writing the epistle, but it is a noun: a pen is a female swan.
explanation.definitionFit: Swansea is the second-largest city in Wales, on the south coast.

clue.text: Perhaps Rev. Spooner's butterflies, skippers, etc?

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so initial sounds are exchanged

blocks.note: butterflies and skippers are relatives of the moth, a family or clan of it

explanation.surface: Rev. Spooner as an amateur lepidopterist with his collection of butterflies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rev. Spooner' reads as one name, but 'Perhaps Rev.' is the definition and 'Spooner's' the instruction; skippers are a family of small butterflies.
explanation.definitionFit: A man of the cloth is a clergyman, and Rev., short for Reverend, is the title given to one.

clue.text: A key held aloft, cryptic Arthurian figure

indicators.note: something cryptic is coded or obscured, so the letters are scrambled out of their plain order

blocks.note: thirteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A mysterious figure from the Round Table stories raising something high, just as she raised Excalibur from the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cryptic' looks like a description of the figure, but it is the instruction to rearrange; the surface cleverly evokes her arm lifting the sword.
explanation.definitionFit: In Arthurian legend the enchantress who gives Arthur his sword Excalibur and later receives it back is known by this title.

clue.text: No time for getting tied up in pastime

indicators.note: saying there is none of something means it must be taken away

blocks.note: becoming knotted or twisted together
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A busy person complaining they have no time to get caught up in a hobby.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the T for time from TANGLING; the surface fittingly hints at fishing lines getting tangled.
explanation.definitionFit: Angling, fishing with rod and line, is one of Britain's most popular leisure hobbies.

clue.text: Some bigwig ran a dancehall in Spanish city

indicators.note: some means only a portion, so the letters are a part of the run of words that follows

blocks.note: spans the end of one word, two whole words and the start of the last

explanation.surface: A local big shot once ran a dance hall in a Spanish city.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across bigwiG RAN A DAncehall.
explanation.definitionFit: Granada is a city in Andalusia, southern Spain, famous for the Alhambra palace.

clue.text: Rose, shunning society, travelled by canoe

indicators.note: to shun is to avoid or keep away from, so something is left out

blocks.note: rose as the past tense of rise: climbed high
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: A woman named Rose avoids company by paddling off alone in a canoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like a name or a flower but is the verb, SOARED; dropping S leaves the answer. Canoes use paddles, so the definition is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: To oar is to propel a boat with oars, so oared means rowed or paddled along on water.

clue.text: 'Differently honestly'?

indicators.note: done differently means done in another way, so the letters are arranged in another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: Rearranging HONESTLY gives ON THE SLY, and acting in a way other than honestly is exactly what the phrase means.
explanation.definitionFit: On the sly is an idiom for secretly or furtively, the opposite of acting openly and truthfully.

clue.text: Time to study Scott, perhaps – lecturer's wanting to hold back

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so something is missing

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to read a subject is to study it at university
Sir Walter Scott, the Scottish novelist, is one bearer of this first name
L is the abbreviation for lecturer

explanation.surface: A lecturer wants to postpone the moment when students study Scott's novels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scott' is a first name here, WALTER, not the surname or the explorer; take the L away for WATER.
explanation.definitionFit: To tread water is an idiom for staying in place without advancing, marking time rather than moving forward.

clue.text: Copy published after T S Eliot initially conceals act of plagiarism

indicators.note: initially means at the beginning, so just the opening letters of the words are wanted
one thing coming after another places it next in line
to conceal is to hide inside, so one part is placed within another

blocks.note: the poet's initials plus the first letter of his surname
a paper that ran a story published it
to crib is to copy someone else's work

explanation.surface: A poem printed under T S Eliot's name turns out to hide a case of plagiarism.
explanation.walkthrough: The newspaper word follows the first initial, and the remaining two initials wrap around the cheating word. To crib is schoolroom slang for copying.
explanation.definitionFit: To transcribe is to write out or reproduce text, so it is a synonym of duplicating or writing out again.

clue.text: Farmyard youngster that's just over a foot

blocks.note: first meaning: a young cow or bull
second meaning: the fleshy back of the lower leg, above the foot

explanation.walkthrough: 'Just over a foot' sounds like a measurement of the young animal's height, but it is a location on the body.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a newborn bovine animal and the muscle at the back of the human shin.

clue.text: Slightly smelly Greek characters felt shame finally in unexpected ways

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so the closing letters of the preceding words are taken

blocks.note: food that is going off starts to smell
pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet, so two or more are pis
the closing letters of both words

explanation.surface: Some Greek people, a little whiffy, felt ashamed when things went oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' means letters of the alphabet, not people; Greek pi in the plural gives PIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Off-piste, from skiing away from groomed runs, is used figuratively for departing from the usual or expected course.

clue.text: Characters in expensive picture, Ben-Hur perhaps

indicators.note: letters contained within the words are the ones to use

blocks.note: spans the last letter of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: The cast of a costly film, such as the chariot-racing Ben-Hur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' suggests the cast of the film but means letters: expensivE PICture.
explanation.definitionFit: Ben-Hur, the 1959 Charlton Heston film, is a classic example of the lavish, long, large-scale historical film genre.

clue.text: Everyman blushes, admitting sanitation ultimately neglected

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so the closing letter is the one taken
to admit is to let in, so one piece is taken inside the other

blocks.note: the setter refers to himself, so in his own words that is I
to blush is to go red, so with 'I' it reads 'I go red'
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: The setter goes pink with embarrassment that the toilets were not looked after.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is the setter of this puzzle, so he is I; I GO RED takes in N to give I G(N)O RED.
explanation.definitionFit: To ignore something is to pay it no attention, so ignored and neglected are synonyms.

clue.text: Girl – not a medallist, we're told – to make a sudden rush

indicators.note: what we are told is heard spoken, so the sound is what counts

blocks.note: a female first name
medals go to first, second and third, so the next place gets none

explanation.surface: A young athlete who just missed a medal suddenly dashes off.
explanation.walkthrough: Coming fourth is the classic near-miss; it sounds like FORTH.
explanation.definitionFit: To sally forth originally meant to make a military charge out of a besieged position, so a sudden dash outward.

clue.text: Artist putting blame on shade of brown, that's not unknown

indicators.note: placing one thing on another sets them side by side in sequence
saying something is not there means it is removed

blocks.note: to take the rap is to take the blame
a light greenish-brown colour, often of eyes
in algebra x, y and z stand for unknowns

explanation.surface: A painter blames a particular brown pigment for a poor result.
explanation.walkthrough: Mathematical unknowns are x, y and z; here it is the Z in HAZEL that goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Raphael was an Italian High Renaissance painter, one of the great masters alongside Leonardo and Michelangelo.

clue.text: Popular actors take these weapons

blocks.note: first meaning, read whimsically: well-loved performers stay at curtain call bending low for an extended time
second meaning: tall bows used by medieval English archers

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a cryptic description: crowd favourites linger at the curtain call; split the answer as LONG BOWS to see it.
explanation.definitionFit: The longbow, a tall yew bow, was the famous weapon of English archers at Crécy and Agincourt.

clue.text: Chicken serving one rejected in French city

indicators.note: something rejected is thrown out, so it is removed

blocks.note: a typical portion of chicken
a means one

explanation.surface: A diner in France sends back a chicken dish.
explanation.walkthrough: The single A is dropped from the chicken portion.
explanation.definitionFit: Brest is a port city at the western tip of Brittany, home to a major French naval base.

clue.text: Schoolchild's twisted effrontery, rebellious

indicators.note: twisted round means turned about, so the order runs backwards

blocks.note: lip is cheek or impudence
a population that is up is in revolt

explanation.surface: A schoolboy's cheek has turned into outright rebellion.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-S means 'is'; LIP + UP read backwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil is a child or young person being taught at school, so it is a synonym for student.

clue.text: Culinary ingredient regularly extracted from saccharin

indicators.note: taking at regular intervals means every other letter is pulled out

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A cooking ingredient routinely derived from an artificial sweetener.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the even letters of sAcChArIn.
explanation.definitionFit: Açaí is a purple berry from an Amazonian palm, used in smoothie bowls and desserts.

clue.text: After disruption, setter's most brusque

indicators.note: something disrupted is thrown into disorder, so the letters come out in a new sequence

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A crossword setter becomes curt after being interrupted.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-S belongs to the material, giving seven letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Terse means curt and short-spoken, so its superlative is a synonym of most abrupt.

clue.text: Cassock's slightly altered for cavalryman

indicators.note: an altered item has been changed, so its letters are rearranged; just a little, since only two swap

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A priest's robe is given minor tailoring so a horse soldier can wear it.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the A and O change places, which is why the change is 'slightly' made.
explanation.definitionFit: Cossacks were horsemen of the Russian and Ukrainian steppes, famed as light cavalry in the Tsar's armies.

clue.text: Entered, dimly tingling with purpose

indicators.note: tingling suggests something agitated and stirred up, so the letters are mixed

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone walks into a dark room, nerves tingling, intent on a mission.
explanation.walkthrough: The twelve letters of the first two words are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting determinedly means acting with resolve and firm intention, so the adverb matches purposefully.
